I used the following source to get me started: https://www.linuxfoundation.org/blog/blog/classic-sysadmin-how-to-rescue-a-non-booting-grub-2-on-linux

My main issue was the command root=/dev/sda1

Despite what others have claimed, this has nothing to do with the period/dot ( . ) at the end of the URL. It is even weirder. Tested this on Safari (Version 26.6.2 (21624.5.1.11.3)) on macOS but I don’t think this has anything to do with browsers. Read on!

That said, this is all very odd and I think it has to do with URL encoding of the link. The link that works is this:

Note the tilde ( ~ ) here: #:~:text= .

Now when you set it as a link, even on this site (like via this URL ), it seems to render the URL as:

Note how the tilde ( ~ ) is gone and replaced with: #:%7E:text= .

Why this happens on some links is anyone’s guess. But whoever runs the site having issues might need to exclude tidle’s ( ~ ) from the URL renderer.

The following sequence of lyrics are found in the song "Give Me a Highway" by American singer-songwriter John Kilzer, which was released in 1989:

Give me a runway, Give me a license-dispenser, Give me a free day.

I’m struggling to figure out what “licence dispenser” means. My first research (dictionaries and etymological databases) shows no standard idiomatic usage.

Is it a malaprop? I thought maybe the transcription was wrong and the lyric was actually "licensed dispenser" (a phrase usually used in medical or pharmaceutical contexts), but neither the phonetics of the track nor the thematic context of the song (which is an anthem of highway travel and nomadic freedom) support that interpretation.

Is it a poetic 'impossible object'? Given the imagery surrounding it, the 'runways' and 'free days', is this a familiar case of poetic license, where an author creates a compound noun to evoke an abstract wish for unbridled freedom?

Is there some cultural idiom I’m not aware of? Could it be a dated regional Americanism or an 80s slang word that has since gone out of common use?

I don't want an easy answer as to what the song means, but an analysis of whether 'licence dispenser' has any linguistic value, or is just a stylistic invention. Have you come across this construction in other literature or songwriting?

I've lived in Salford all my life and people from The City of Manchester say the Salfordian accent has a scouse twinge to it and I think they are probably correct.

A scouse twinge after all just means your parents, grandparents or great grandparents came from Ireland. And a lot of Irish settled in Salford especially in the Ordsall area after the building of the Liverpool to Manchester railway, the Bridgewater Canal and the Manchester ship canal.

But I can tell you now, to me Andy Burnham just sounds pure 100% scouse. It's not even one of those fake Scouse accents that teens from Wigan and Tyldesley put on until they grow up and realise they should just speak with the normal accent for that area.

No single feature of speech can be used to say a person is speaking a dialect .

This question is about sociolect : In sociolinguistics, a sociolect or social dialect is a variety of language (a register) used by a socioeconomic class, a profession, an age group or other social group.

sociolect

If an otherwise educated speaker - a speaker who claims to be educated or is recognized by others as being educated - says: I should have went or I have went , they are speaking outside of their sociolect's register. That aspect of their speech is sub-standard.

So, if one wants to determine whether or not a person is coherent within a register, there has to be more than a single feature that decides that.

Here is an article on dialects and sociolects in England, but the ideas apply to AmE as well. [not actual AmE speech]. Dialects and sociolects cannot be detected by a single item, such as Have + Past Participle.

Piece of junk refers to something that is cheap, shoddy, or worthless. It can be used as an oject as in "This piece of junk won't boot." or a modiying adjective as in "This piece-of-junk computer won't boot" (with or without hyphens).

Related adjectives can be used with the name of the device. These include

Junky Shoddy Trashy Lousy Worthless Crappy (Oh, and, of course, "shitty".)
links.after:
Piece of junk refers to something that is cheap, shoddy, or worthless. It can be used as an oject as in "This piece of junk won't boot." or a modiying adjective as in "This piece-of-junk computer won't boot" (with or without hyphens).

Related adjectives can be used with the name of the device. These include

Junky Shoddy Trashy Lousy Worthless Crappy (Oh, and, of course, "shitty".)

Boat Anchor which merely means the device is only suitable for that purpose. "This computer has become a boat anchor" ([Urban Dictionary, definitions 2 and 3][1], [Ham.net][2] shows the term used in practice.)

Doorstop similar to "boat anchor". "This computer only works as a door stop now."

Junk Box No longer suitable for anything except to be cannibalized for spare parts. ([See wikipedia.][3]) Usually this refers to just the parts themselves, already disassembled and collected into a box. But it parallels your German reference, so I thought it was worth adding.

We also refer to some things as "hanger queens", which is alludes to aircraft that spend more time in repair than they do in service. Any products that can't get through the production process may be relegated to being hangar queens, with hopes that someone will eventually figure out how to repair them.

This problem started with the first attempt starting the furnace this season. The furnace is rather old.

The pilot light is lit, and it works fine. However, when the heat call comes, the gas starts to flow for an instant, and then the pilot goes out. It is possible that the main burner also briefly (fraction of a second) lights before it all goes out.

Ideas? TIA
links.after:
This problem started with the first attempt starting the furnace this season. The furnace is rather old.

The pilot light is lit, and it works fine. However, when the heat call comes, the gas starts to flow for an instant, and then the pilot goes out. It is possible that the main burner also briefly (fraction of a second) lights before it all goes out.

--- UPDATE The pilot light sensor was changed 3 years ago - it does seem to be sensing and working since the pilot light remains lit, and needs to be heated a bit before it stays on.

I also confirmed that the 24VAC solenoid in the valve is switching (outside of the system). However, I wasn't able to confirm that the valve was open outside the system - as it clearly needs more than just an electrical signal to open the valve. Unfortunately I didn't test it in the system by applying the 24VAC like I did outside. Guess I'll put it back in the system to see.

Ideas? TIA

I just bought a home with a hot tub/pool in the backyard, and the hot tub is slightly elevated over the pool, and designed so that water will flow over the side of the tub and into the pool below (kind of like an infinity pool). I’ve noticed fairly large cracks in the top of the concrete wall of the hot tub and some of the water is flowing down into those cracks, rather than over the top and into the pool. My concern is that the water is causing erosion inside the wall, and if left unchecked, it will eventually collapse. The previous owners said it’s been in this state for a couple years (offer was as-is so I’m on my own for the cost, unfortunately).

I’ve had three contractors out to examine it and all three have said that it can’t be simply repaired, and will need to be torn down and rebuilt. Quotes range from $30-50k so I’m not keen to do the work in the short term. One of the contractors said it can probably be reinforced (via injecting epoxy or some other adhesive into the crack) and may last for years with this fix, but wouldn’t be able to guarantee anything.

Since the absolute worst case here is the wall collapsing (at which point I’d need to hire someone to rebuild it anyway), I’m inclined to go with the “reinforce” route in the short term. My plan is as follows:

Inject Loctite PL Premium as deep as possible into the cracks to strengthen the wall

Fill the gaps on top where cement has chipped away with 3M Bondo Putty to create a smooth surface

Coat the top with Gor

Steel framing components may seem somewhat flimsy on an individual basis, but once assembled into a double-sheathed wall are more than strong enough for tile. The load of tile is almost entirely in sheer, so there's really no bending force applied to the wall.

Your key concerns are fastening to the steel in a way that's appropriate. Make sure you were using the correct screws with the correct thread pitch, and so on.

If you did feel like you need to add strength, simply sister some 2x4 studs alongside the steel studs and attach them with pairs of screws every 16 to 24 inches. The wood studs should be alongside the primary flange of the steel studs, not the hollow side. They do not need to be full height, just as long as you can fit.

I am planning/working on turning my unfinished basement into a mostly finished space. I have done a fair bit of research to make sure I am doing everything correctly, but am stuck on how to properly insulate a rim joist cavity that is partially inaccessible.

Some background: I live in the Denver Metro area, so the climate is very dry. I still want to make sure I am mitigating moisture properly, and plan to insulate the concrete walls with XPS to provide both a thermal barrier and a moisture barrier.

For the rim joists, I am between doing cut XPS and spray foaming the gaps to get a full air seal, or using 2 part closed cell spray foam to get a 2" layer in the rim joist bay. Both options would likely be supplemented with some new batt insulation to get the R value up a little. The latter option would just be to save time from cutting multiple uniquely sized XPS pieces, and is the option I am leaning towards. Regardless, I have a set of rim joists that run parallel to the concrete wall that is nearly on top of said wall. The access behind the rim joist is extremely limited, in particular along one ~12foot long joist. At that joist I have about 2"of clearance, and no room for a hand or tool to get behind it. The other joist have slightly more clearance, and I can stick a hand up there. The cavity is about 8-9" deep, 9" tall. This cavity already has fiberglass batt insulation in it, but it is 50 years old and not in great shape. To make matters more difficult, the HVAC trunks bu

I open Firefox, click "maximize" button at the top right of the main window, then "minimize" then "maximize" again, then every attempt to maximize the window will give the same result: the window is shifted a few pixels down. There's a white stripe above the window (it's unclickable), and a transparent stripe above that white stripe, I can click windows behind it. The bottom of the window is hidden behind the taskbar.

Acer V3-574G-54UH, Windows 10

Graphics Hardware: Intel i5-5200U and Nvidia 940M.

This is how it looks.

links.before: I couldn't get the method based on the keyboard creator to work. Instead, I came up with an AutoHotKey script. The method for detecting the current keyboard layout is taken from How to find out what is the current keyboard layout?
links.after:
I couldn't get the method based on the keyboard creator to work. Instead, I came up with an AutoHotKey script. The method for detecting the current keyboard layout is taken from How to find out what is the current keyboard layout? .

The idea is to automate sending the sequence "dead key + space". Since this will have the wrong effect for layouts without dead keys, I filter based on the locale ID, which for the German keyboard fulfills the pattern 0x0407???? . This value may not be portable, given that keyboard layouts are not hardcoded.

I considered using GetKeyboardLayoutNameA , but the value sometimes is outdated.

In the News on the Web corpus, there are 73 hits for about the (plural noun)' (-ing verb) , so version with a genitive plural noun (not a pronoun) is not non-existent.

However, there are 15672 hits for the same without the apostrophe after the plural noun, so this construction is quite definitely not the standard. Searching for a similar string with a wildcard for the preposition - (preposition) (plural noun)' (-ing verb) - in the Corpus of Contemporary American English we get 102 hits for the version with the preposition and 2000 for the one without.

There is also the issue of whether the non-genitive NP (no apostrophe) is interpreted as the subject of a gerund-participle (- ing clause) or whether the gerund-participle is interpreted a post-head dependent in an NP headed by the plain form noun. For example,

where we could understand "the students who steal the test papers" or "the fact that the students are stealing test papers" / "the possibility that the students will steal test papers" / etc.

But even so, with ratios like the ones above, it's hard to recommend the version with the apostrophe - on the contrary it would probably be best to advise against it unless the writer is 100% confident they need it and know what they're doing.

One pretty near universally applicable option would be to negate the matrix clause and emphasize (in speech) the first word in the adjunct (your adverbial) to make clear that this is what is being negated and not the content of the matrix clause generally, or to negate the head word of the adjunct directly; but of course you would typically also have to supply a correct substitution for the negated element - not A but B - unless the context made it abundantly clear.

Sometimes it's not the head word that would have to be emphasized, but rather whatever shows the contrast.

Of course there are still limitations, for example I've found no examples of correcting an although... with another although... , though as in the examples above it is possible to correct it with another word.

I have read that in English, reason adverbial clauses introduced by because can be focalized using the it is... that... cleft construction, whereas those introduced by since resist such focalization (The Cambridge Grammar of the English Language, 2002, p. 732). This observation leads me to the following question: When someone offers a causal explanation for an event using a because -clause, and I wish to rebut their assertion about the cause—that is, to sever the link between the because -clause and the main clause—what I am doing semantically amounts to saying that the proposition in the because-clause is not the cause. This constitutes a negation of the causal relation itself, rather than a negation of the content within the causal clause while preserving the causal relation. To put it concretely, it is not transforming:

I am very angry because he ate my cake.

into:

I am very angry because he didn’t eat my cake.

Rather, it means excluding “he ate my cake” from the set of all possible causes for “I am very angry.” Returning now to the contrast between because and since : if the speaker’s reason clause is introduced by since , and I want to rebut them by denying the connection between the main clause and the proposed cause, then—given that since -clauses cannot be focalized via the it is... that... structure—I apparently cannot construct a corresponding negative cleft ( it isn’t... that... ). In such cases, what negation operator should I use instead?

More broadly, I don

Note that this answer applies equally to " two more things/units " vs. " two things/units more ". Also: the choice between "fewer" (for nonsingular nouns) and "less" (for singular nouns) is an independent issue.

When a numerically quantified noun phrase receives a measure construal, the NP as a whole functions as a measure phrase, and the first construction is somewhat marked relative to the second. When it receives a count construal, the first construction is slightly more direct and may be preferable to the second, though both constructions are idiomatic.

When the relevant quantities have different units, the first construction is strongly preferred.

Today "multiple" is widely used as a synonym for "many," fancy jargon, in my opinion, to say "more than one."

Is there any support for a more precise meaning or connotation to stand instead for the repetition or multiplication of an element of a whole?

Oxford, cited below, defines the word as "having or involving several parts, elements, or members," consistent with this sense of the word. At the threads below, we see that Merriam-Webster comes and and says "multiple" means "consisting of, including, or involving more than one." The examples M-W gives reflect a sense of parts of a whole or duplicates: "multiple births" and "multiple choice."

Many people use "multiple" in multiple contexts, so this is hard to search! ELU threads here and here come at multiple in different ways, but neither addresses my question.

First, "more than one" and "many" are acceptable meanings for " multiple ."

We could stop there, but we can do better. "Multiple," many authorities and kibitzers contend, is best used to describe separation, repetition, or division from a whole. Most of Merriam-Webster's definition carry this idea of repetition. Michael Kandel of the MLA agrees`:

A deft writer can express herself vividly by precisely using "multiple" when it's called for. It's correct to use "multiple" to mean "more than one," but I think it's less than industrious.

In my experience, in the past twenty years writers have come to use "multiple" as a fancier, more authoritative way to say "many." Kandel suggests that this usage fits squarely into Bryan Garner's definition of jargon: use the longer word when the shorter one will do.

In a stale thread in English Forward , more than a few (and here I might well say "multiple," though "many" or "a lot" is fine) commenters vent on the bloated use of "multiple." One mirrors the prescriptive, grumpy old man in me, at least on this topic:

(I'm not sure, but English Forward appears to be British.)

Note : This is a question about the absence of the aorist tense in the English language and the complication of rendering, accurately, the correct tense when translating form other languages.

It is not a question about the Greek (or any other) language.

I have noticed translators having difficulty in representing an active aorist participle in English and I am pondering how it should be done, correctly.

In 1 John 5:6 the Koine Greek phrase outos estin o elthon (ουτος εστιν ο ελθων) contains the active aorist participle, elthon (ελθων) and various attempts have been made to accurately represent this in English, preserving the precise meaning.

The Authorised King James version, the J N Darby version and the Englishman's Greek New Testament (interlinear, literal) all give the rendering 'this is he that came'.

Robert Young, who strove ater exactitude at the expence of readability, has 'this is one who did come'.

The recent John Metcalfe version gives us 'this is the one coming' which clearly wants us to have a participle, of sorts ; but, to me, that has a future meaning (unless that is a matter of my own local idiomaticy).

My own attempt also gives a participle but attempts to represent the active aorist meaning with the word 'once' - 'this is he [once] coming'.

I am still not clear as to how we can, in English , express an active aorist participle and accurately convey both the verbal activity of the participle but also the concept of a once-completed action.

Greek Aori

My town also has a requirement that any source of ignition be 18 inches above the floor, so I put a pellet stove in my workshop's garage on a new "floor" 19 inches above the concrete floor. I built a platform of standard hollow concrete blocks (8x8x16) with a top layer of solid cap units, so it's just 2 blocks high plus the cap layer.

I used construction adhesive formulated for masonry. It was super easy, and the whole thing went together in less than an hour. It has been in place for 11 years with no issues.

For you, this would satisfy both the 18-inch requirement and the Rinnai requirement that the heater be mounted on a floor.

In your case, that's not too bad since your key doesn't have a password (although I would caution against that as well, of course). Otherwise, on first launch, of course, it will start a new agent.

Done

There you have it. The SSH agent is started automatically for each terminal. The keys are automatically added but only on first use in that terminal. Only then the passphrase is asked, so only once in that terminal.

Is there an easy way to assign the current document’s text to a JavaScript variable?

Ideally, a one-liner such as: const sDocTxt = document.Text; or const sDocTxt = document.GetText();

My current approach is to retrieve each line with document.GetLine(iLine); and join them into an array.

Caveat: The command must not change the selection. I.e. document.selection.SelectAll(); is not an option.

Looking at the product website

USB PD for most part is universal, and you can use any USB PD charger that can supply an appropriate amount of power - the system comes packed in with a 65W adaptor so any charger or powerbank that supports USB PD and has a wattage of 65W or better should work.

I've successfully run a USB PD capable convertable (a surface pro 7) via a USB PD powerbank. The powercore 20100 is not a USB PD capable powerbank - the anker website lists it as only supporting 5v, and is unlikely to work at all.

Using winget, I installed the latest LibreOffice (LibreOffice 25.2.3.2) using --scope machine , with the intention of making LibreOffice available for all users that log into each workstation:

But, I've discovered that in order for a logged-in user to successfully launch LibreOffice, they first have to launch it in safe-mode and then disable hardware acceleration:

You can't just do this once, as administrator, and consider it done. Every user of the workstation must do this the very first time they launch LibreOffice.

Naturally, I'm very disappointed that the LibreOffice developers haven't discovered a mechanism by which they can reliably detect if hardware acceleration is succeeding and disable this setting automatically if it isn't.

It is unreasonable to put this burden on my users. So, my question is:

How can I installed LibreOffice, for all user of each workstation, where hardware acceleration is turned OFF by default for all users (which includes new users who will be logging in for the first time)?

Adding to Tony's very good answer :

There have been multiple bug reports and feature requests on the qBittorrent Github over the past decade regarding this and similar/related issues. Work has been done on them, but no clear solution. It appears QB tried implementing a .unwanted folder at one point where unwanted files could be placed and these would not be downloaded, but that was removed due to being buggy and unreliable.

In one of these it was noted that the capabilities of QB are largely dependent on Libtorrent , the library QB is heavily based upon, and such a feature may need to be requested there, rather in QB itself.

While you may have had some success doing this yourself (judging from comments, which info was not in the original question) in the past, that may have been by accident, or on a version of the software in which they were experimenting with the capability.

I have my Windows laptop connected to a Linux computer using a CAT 6 ethernet cable, negotiated link speed is 1000Mbps Duplex. Linux computer uses a external USB Rj45 port instead of a internal one, capable of up to 1.25Gbps speed while the Windows laptop uses a build in Rj45 port capable of up to 1000Mbps.

Problem is when I run iperf3 on them to test speed, I first started with Linux as the client and Windows as the server, resulted in a speed of 940Mbps which is expected, however if I do it in reverse with Linux as server the speed only goes up to 600Mbps . So what can possibly cause it?

Test results:

CPU/RAM usage is fine on both device, did not max out.

The Linux Computer does handle other network traffic from other devices as well and acts as a router and do all the NAT and PPPoE Dial, but that is from a completely different physical Rj45 port so I think it is irrelevant, hence not gonna paste the Iptables and routing rules here.

Surely only one signal can traverse a wire at once so wouldn't the largest frequency be used all of the time. I can see why a large a bandwidth is good for wireless communication as the different frequencies differentiate between different communications.

To my untrained eye these two look different from real pluralia-tantum nouns like eg. "riches" and most probably different from e.g. "dregs", for which (however rare) a correct singular "dreg" exists. I have to admit, however, that I cannot substantiate this gut-feeling.

Addendum:

Yes, it is possible to use e.g. "statistic" as a singular, but that is not my point. What I am interested in is the fact that "statistics" is used as a singular (like in Statistics is the use of ... ) although being clearly the plural form of the word. Since the word looks like a Latin loan word and it seems to have been taken into English in its singular and plural form there must have been (I suppose) some development(s) leading to the plural form being used as a singular too. I am interested in precisely these developments.

I wonder in what context native speakers would actually use the sentence that way. Have you ever heard people say anything similar?
